text:
R. v. Carman, 2001 ABPC            82

Date:
20010419

Docket:
06695142P10101

06967111P10101

05659354P10101

15050545P10101

IN
THE PROVINCIAL COURT OF ALBERTA

CRIMINAL
DIVISION

BETWEEN:

HER
MAJESTY THE QUEEN

-
and -

EVERETTE
SHANNON CARMAN

REASONS
FOR SENTENCE OF

THE
HONOURABLE JUDGE S. L. VAN DE VEEN

Counsel:
M. Daoust, Esq., for the Crown

D.G. Yanko, Esq., for the Accused

ADMITTED FACTS

[
1
]        The accused has
entered a guilty plea to the charge of robbery contrary to s. 344(b) of the
Code, along with  guilty pleas to two charges of theft under $5,000.00 contrary
to s.334(b) of the Code.  He also entered guilty pleas to one charge of
obstructing a security guard contrary to s. 139(2) of the Code and a charge of
failing to attend court contrary to s.145(2)(a) of the Code.

[
2
]        The most serious
of the charges is the robbery. The admitted facts to that charge are that on
May 1
st
, 2000 the accused entered the Scotia Bank in Calgary at 1:00
p.m.  He presented a holdup note to the bank teller, Carol McQueen.  The note
stated he was in possession of a gun and that he wanted $15,000.  The note also
contained a threat to kill people if he did not get his way.  He verbally told
the teller not to push any buttons and he then waited as the victim went into
the counting room to get the money.  The victim there informed another employee
of the robbery and the police were notified via the 9-1-1 phone line.  An off
duty police officer, Constable Steele, happened to be present in the bank when
the robbery was taking place and he became suspicious of the accused’s actions.  The bank manager also became aware of
what was going on and told the accused he ought to take what was available and
leave.  The teller placed the money from her drawer in the binder provided by
the accused and he then fled the  bank.  He was pursued by Constable Steele,
the bank manager and a bank customer.

[
3
]        There were two
other males standing lookout for the accused and waiting by a vehicle.  They
fled on foot.  In an effort to elude being captured the accused threw the money
across the parking lot.  Some $6,950.00 was recovered by the bank leaving a
shortage of $1,547.00.  The accused was then immediately apprehended in the
parking lot.

[
4
]        The next offense
to which the accused has entered a guilty plea, being a theft under $5,000.00 ,
took place on October 26, 2000, while the accused was out on judicial interim
release.  At  approximately 1:00 p.m. the accused entered the Bata Athlete’s World Outlet in Deerfoot Mall in North East
Calgary.  Once inside he selected a pair of black boots and a Columbia jacket.
He exited the store into the mall without paying for the items and was
approached by store security.  He gave some resistence to store  security who
apprehended him, but was handcuffed when police arrived and then calmed down.
The property taken was valued at $349.98.

[
5
]        The second theft charge before the Court
occurred on December 2, 2000.  On

this date the accused, two
black males, and one black female were in the Kal Tire store in North East
Calgary at approximately 12:30 p.m., just after lunch.  An employee observed
the males select three high performance tires and carry them outside the main
entrance door. They placed them into the back of a red truck.  The employee confronted
the accused and one of the other males ran from the scene.  The employee was
able to recover the stolen tires from the truck  The accused said he was there
picking up tires for a friend and when the employee tried to get the license
plate number of the truck, the accused stood in front of it and the employee
moved him to the side so he could get the license plate number.  The accused
then jumped into the truck and drove off.

[
6
]     The next charge before the Court is a
failure to attend court on December 13,

2000, and the accused
admits to having failed to attend court for the trial of a theft charge dated
December 19, 1999, a charge which the Crown has withdrawn.

[
7
]     The last  charge
before the Court is a charge of obstruction of justice charge, specifically
pertaining to the interference with the duties of a security guard, contrary to
Section 139(2) of the Code.  Facts relating to this charge are that on January
10
th
, 2001, at 3:40 p.m.  the accused entered the A & B Sound
store in North East Calgary in the company of a female.  Inside they conversed
for several minutes and then split up.  The accused exited the store and about
five minutes later the female, named Smith, exited the store carrying a bag.
When she exited, the security alarm went off.  One Mathew Harrison, a security
guard, saw this occur and  followed Smith.  She threw the bag under a vehicle
in the parking lot.  Harrison then approached her and told her she was under
arrest for theft and he requested that she follow him back into the store.  The
accused then intervened and grabbed Harrison by the arm.  Harrison identified
himself as store security and told the accused the female was a thief.  The
accused continued to block Harrison and hang onto him, trying to prevent him
from taking the female back into the store.  The accused and Smith then walked
away from Harrison, refusing to come back into the store.  The police were
nearby and were able to assist Harrison in bringing the two back into the
store.  The accused and Smith were both arrested.  The value of the goods Smith
had in the bag was $500.00.

POSITIONS OF CROWN
AND DEFENCE

[
8
]     The Crown seeks a global sentence of four
years incarceration.  The Crown

submits that thefts from a
financial institution have in the past generally attracted a four year
penitentiary term in cases of this kind where there has been a threat with a
note saying the offender had a gun.  The Crown points out that the accused was
on judicial interim release at the time each of the other charges before the
Court took place.  The Crown also points out with respect to the theft from Kal
Tire that the accused, even when caught, dishonestly tells the store employee a
story, saying he is there to pick the tires up for a friend.  The Crown further
points out with respect to the obstruction of justice charge on January 10
th

that the accused attempted to prevent the female from getting caught after she
steals $500.00 worth of CDs at a time he has been in the store with her.

[
9
]     Defence initially set forward the view that
a sentence of three to three and a half

years globally would be
appropriate in this case.  However, at a subsequent sentencing hearing to the
one held on January 24, 2001 the defence changed its position.  Defence now
seek  a conditional sentence order which would permit the accused to serve his
sentence in the community.  The accused has now been in custody for
approximately four months, having been arrested on January 10
th
,
2001 and ordered detained.

[
10
]   The issue before the Court is whether a
conditional sentence is appropriate in the

circumstances of this case.

PERSONAL
CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE ACCUSED SURROUNDING THE OFFENSE

[
11
]   The accused was 18
years old at the time of the robbery.  He was born September 29, 1981 and was
therefore 19 at the time some of the other offenses before the Court took
place.  He has completed most of the courses for grade 11 in school and had
worked at the family business known as Carman’s Hair Studio until differences of opinion between himself and his
family occurred and he was required to leave the family home.  This took place
in early 2000, prior to the robbery and other offenses before the Court.

[
12
]   This case involves
some unusual evidence presented at the sentencing hearing.  The accused’s father testified and told the Court that until 10
years ago he had not been a good father.  In fact he had been a drug dealer and
had gone to gaol for it and had, for the past ten years reformed his
lifestyle.  He testified that his family were now his main concern.  It was
evident from listening to him that he was making genuine attempts to overcome
his past and to be a better father.  He also stated that his son had been the
subject of racial slurs in High River, which accounts for the prior youth court
record of the accused.  Apparently this is a Jewish family and his son was
called a “dirty Jew”.  The accused is a young man who is physically
slight.  There is some evidence he was the subject of bullying in school and
from my observation of him, his physical appearance is such that he could well
be the target of bullying in future as well.  He is small and looks younger
than his age.  He also has something of a baby face.

[
13
]  According to Gary
Carman, the accused’s father, he told
his son to leave the home at a time the boy had nowhere to go.  As a result he
went to live with a family who Mr. Carman, Sr. had helped at an earlier time.
This family had been the subject of racial prejudice and Mr. Carman had helped
their  children.  They showed the accused the wrong ways in the words of Mr.
Carman and all of the offenses which the accused committed were as a result of
his being under the influence of this family.  He was “used” in the
words of Mr. Carman, and frankly, it is not difficult to understand the accused
trying to fit in and please a family who extended their hands to him when he
had been ordered to leave his own home and had nowhere else to go.  It is not
difficult to imagine him choosing their ways during this time frame of his
life.

[
14
]   I recognize that the
heartfelt grief of a parent who testified on behalf of their child in a
criminal proceeding such as this is natural and to be expected, but there is
some depth to the remarks of Mr. Carman, Sr. in this case which I feel are
important.  Firstly, he believes he made a gross error in ordering his son out
of the house when he had nowhere to go and secondly he recognizes that in his
earlier years he had not been the kind of father he would have liked.  While
this latter point may be true for many people who have the benefit of hindsight
at middle age, this is particularly true in a case where the father has been
imprisoned for dealing in cocaine.  The accused  unfortunately did not have a
law abiding father in his formative years but it is obvious that his father
now, and for the last ten years or so, is determined to do all he can to undo
the harm his previous lifestyle caused to his family.  This appears to be a family
which has many obstacles to overcome and is making progress in addressing them
in a positive way.

[
15
]   The accused’s entire family were present in court for the
January 24th sentencing hearing.  His mother was present along with his 20 year
old sister, Danielle,  and 15 year old brother.  His mother suffers from Type 2
Diabetes, which is severe in nature and requires care given by other family
members.  The accused has participated in this along with other family
members.  It was not made clear to the Court on January 24
th
how
extensive the care given for the accused’s
mother is.

PRESENTENCE REPORT AND PSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT

[
16
]   According to the
presentence report the accused has two prior criminal convictions, in 1996 and
1999 respectively, both having occurred when he was under the age of 18.  One
was assault with a weapon and the other an assault.  Both offenses resulted in
probationary sentences and were explained by the accused’s father as having arisen because of the accused’s response to racial slurs against him.  This is
consistent with the accused’s report
that the assault with a weapon occurred when he retaliated against a fellow
student who had made anti-Jewish slurs against him, by using a piece of gym
equipment to assault the other student.  The second assault is not explained in
the presentence report, which states that the circumstances surrounding this
assault are unknown.

[
17
]   The accused accepts
responsibility for his actions in these offenses and expresses remorse.  He is
not in a position to make restitution immediately, but he expresses willingness
to offer an apology and make compensation for all losses caused by his
actions.  The accused has been under probationary supervision as a result of
his youth court convictions and has been fully cooperative with probation
authorities.  It was noted that he had problems with anger management and the
accused was referred to the Peter Lougheed Hospital  for anger management
assessment, but the accused failed to follow through with this treatment.
However he was doing well in all areas of his life at the time and was not
charged with breach of probation for this failure.

[
18
]   Between September
1999 and November 1999 Constable Teeter, School Resource Officer, took an
interest in the accused and under his guidance he became involved in school and
community programs which were credited for community service work which the
accused had failed to complete on time.

[
19
]   The presentence
report relates the victim, Carol McQueen’s
thoughts about the accused at the time of the robbery.  She thought the accused
appeared to be very young at the time of the robbery and she felt his actions
would ruin his future.  He did not appear to be “as scary as the stereotype robber”.
Nevertheless she was traumatized by the event and had nightmares for about a
month.  She found the training and support offered by her employer helpful.

[
20
]   The Carman family is
portrayed in some detail in this report, and, as anticipated by the testimony
of Gary Carman, there have been many severe disruptions for this family who
despite great odds are still together as a functioning unit and even providing
a home for a four year old daughter to Danielle (the 20 year old sister of the
accused), a child who was conceived as a result of a sexual assault on her
mother.  The criminal charge in connection with that occurrence is currently
before the courts.  The parents have separated about 15 times.  The father’s criminal past coupled with the mother’s illness and perhaps  related emotional
difficulties which have been described as abusive by the accused have produced
a less than stable environment for this accused.  The determination of this
couple to pursue their marriage and to provide a home for their family is, however,
clear.  The father believes his son felt abandoned by his mother who left the
family often, as well as his father who went to gaol for his criminal
activity.  Mr. Carman now stands behind his son whatever the future holds and
he is committed to always be there until all of his son’s legal difficulties are resolved.  He has respect
for the justice system and indicates that his son will be required to carry out
any instructions or recommendations made by the Court in relation to these
offenses.  My assessment of the accused is that he, too, is prepared to  accept
any sentence handed down in this case and he recognizes the seriousness of his
actions.

[
21
]   Detective Bellion,
the investigating officer described the accused as a very unsophisticated
criminal whose efforts were designed to fail from the start.  The accused has
stated that he knew there would be consequences if he were caught, but he never
realized how difficult serving time at the remand centre would be.  Both the
accused’s father and his sister believe
the accused has learned from a serious error in judgment and that he will not
likely be before the courts again.

[
22
]   The accused appears
to be dependent upon his father for his future work or occupational endeavors.
His father would permit the accused to continue working with his salon, but
there are indications in the reports that the family business may not be strong
financially.  In fact, the accused’s
sister and the accused’s father both
believe the accused’s motivation for
the robbery was to assist the family business financially.  At present the
accused would like to buy cars and restore them in order to sell them at a
profit.  His father is prepared to support him in this goal since the accused
has acquired some experience in autobody work as a result of exposure to this
field through the father of one of his closest friends who is the owner of a
garage.  It is unclear how practical this goal is or what depth the accused has
in terms of experience in this field.

[
23
]   The accused is
described in the presentence report as exhibiting only prosocial values and
respect for the law.  His entire family, while not condoning his actions,
remain  fully supportive of him, and he is considered to be a suitable
candidate for community supervision.

PSYCHOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT

[
24
]   This report
described the accused as a young man with very traditional values who may feel
insecure regarding his masculinity.  He does not pose a high risk to himself or
others, and presented as a person who, having pled guilty to the offenses
before the Court, was waiting to accept responsibility for his actions.  He
does not suffer from any personality disorder, substance abuse problem, or
mental illness.  No further psychiatric follow-up is suggested.

[
25
]   There is some
further detail concerning his parents which explain the lack of stable
judgments made by this accused.  His mother had alcohol and drug problems
through her pregnancy and hemorrhaged in the seventh month.  She carried the
accused to full term but he had to live with his grandmother for the first
three months of his life.  The report describes the accused’s home life as chaotic, involving several moves and
school changes, multiple parental separations, mutual domestic violence, the
mother having left the home several times,  and the father having been
incarcerated for criminal behavior.  His mother has had two psychiatric
admissions within the last three years following suicide attempts.  His father
is confirmed to have taken on the role of protector of his family in recent
years especially following the sexual assault of  Danielle.

[
26
]   The accused
repeatedly underlined and emphasized that he alone was responsible for the
robbery offense.  He confirmed his sister’s
and his father’s opinion of motive for
the robbery, namely that he was attempting to financially rescue his father’s failing hair salon business.  The accused is
resigned to serving time in prison.

REFERENCE LETTERS

[
27
]   Exhibit 2 contains
three reference letters which all indicate that this accused may well respond
to a rehabilitative sentence.  He is described by a former employer as
conscientious and reliable.  Peter Eng, the owner and operator of Abco Services
spoke highly of the accused and indicated a willingness to hire him in future.
He considers the accused an asset to his company.  He was trusted to do bank
deposits and there is no suggestion the accused in any way violated this
trust.  Indeed there is no suggestion of any dishonesty whatsoever and the
accused worked for this employer in both 1999 and 2000 (it is not clear what
part of the year 2000).

[
28
]   Another letter is in
evidence from the accused’s aunt,
Brenda Rubeniuk.  She understandably may be biased, but her letter is
nonetheless of some value in that she describes the accused’s actions as being entirely out of character.  She
describes the help the accused has been to her as a single mother.  She also
relates that the accused has been a contributing member of society and cites an
example where he  helped a lady in Olympic Plaza who was being harassed by an
aggressive drunk.  The accused escorted her to pay her bills and brought her to
the train making sure she was safe.  The accused’s love of and caring for family are mentioned not only by his aunt, but
also the author of a third letter of reference.

AGGRAVATING AND
MITIGATING FACTORS

[
29
]   The primary
aggravating factor is the nature of the robbery offense, namely the robbery of
a financial institution.  It is also an aggravating factor that he then
committed the other offenses while on judicial interim release.  The fact that
he not only committed the thefts, but also obstructed justice by interfering
with the duties of a security guard (by essentially leading the female suspect
away against objections of the security guard) and then failed to attend court
for trial upon yet another theft charge are also aggravating factors.  The need
to protect financial institutions from robbery is obvious as is the trauma such
a robbery can have upon the direct victims of the offense, namely the teller
who is presented with the “note”.  This is a case where there was a threat of
violence and the accused said he had a gun, although  he did not in fact have a
gun.  I have treated the contents of the note as an aggravating factor.

[
30
]   The mitigating
factors are that the accused was a youthful offender, just 18 when the robbery
offense occurred.  His actions were described by the investigating officer as
very unsophisticated, an assessment which is borne out by the facts in the case
indicating that the teller immediately told another employee who called 9-1-1,
and the fact that the accused’s actions
were so suspicious as to attract the attention of an off duty policeman in the
bank at the time.  The accused was chased by three people, indicating he was
not particularly frightening.  He appeared very young to the teller whose
thought at the time of the robbery was he was ruining his life.  He also threw
the money in the parking lot, thereby not gaining financially from the robbery.

[
31
]   It is also a
mitigating factor that the accused entered guilty pleas prior to trial,
although it is noted the matter had been scheduled for preliminary inquiry and
witnesses were called off only at the last when defense advised the Crown
guilty pleas would be tendered to the robbery and other charges.  The accused
also has no prior adult record and his youth record is explained as having
occurred as a result of racial prejudice against Jewish people such as the
accused, at least as far as the assault with a weapon is concerned.

[
32
]   I have also taken
into account as a mitigating factor the circumstances surrounding this offense
which include the father’s explanation
about the accused being told to leave his home even when he had nowhere to go
and the father’s recognition that the
accused then found himself influenced by the only people willing to take him
in, namely a family who were a very poor influence upon him throughout the
entire time frame covering these offenses.  I accept the evidence in the presentence
report that the motive for the robbery was for the accused to rescue his father’s failing hair salon business.

[
33
]   I also note the
accused has spent from January 10
th
, 2001 in pretrial custody and I
have considered this pretrial time to be more difficult than post trial custody
where various programs and work projects are available to prisoners.  I
especially think this pretrial custody has been difficult for this accused who
is not only youthful, but has never spent any time in custody before.  At the
time the presentence report was written (prior to February 28, 2001), it was
already evident the accused had underestimated the difficulty of time in
custody.  This sentencing occurring some months later, in April, I expect the
impression  made upon the accused of incarceration will be that much stronger.

LEGAL AUTHORITIES AND
THEIR APPLICATION

[
34
]   In the decision of
R.
v. Earl
(1985)
A.J. 168
Mr. Justice Laycraft wrote that the robbery of a
financial institution must attract a substantial sentence.  He went on to say
that in  the so-called “robbery by note” cases, the starting point for consideration of the
sentence is four years with adjustments up or down after review of the various
mitigating and aggravating circumstances.  The same thing had been held in

R. v. Kurych
, an unreported decision of the same court.

[
35
]   However, that
leading decision was rendered prior to the amendments to the
Criminal Code

which set forth principles to guide the courts with respect to sentencing and
added the provisions permitting the serving of  gaol sentences in the
community.  Those legislative changes occurred some ten years after
R. v.
Earl
and were recently considered by the Supreme Court of Canada in the
decision of
R. v. Proulx, supra,
(2000)
2000 SCC 5 (CanLII)
,
140 C.C.C. (3d)

449
.
While the facts in that case are entirely different, the Court spent
considerable time reviewing the conditional sentence provisions of the Code
along with the relatively new sentencing provisions enacted in 1995 and set
forth a good deal of guidance for the lower courts on this subject.

[
36
]   In
R. v. Proulx
, supra
the Court
considered s. 718 through to s. 718.2, being the

newly enacted sentencing
principles along with s. 742.1 through to s. 742.6, which relate to the
creation of conditional sentences.  The Court held it was necessary to consider
the new sentencing tool of conditional sentences in the broader context of the
comprehensive sentencing reforms enacted by Bill C-41 as a whole.  At Page 466
the Court states as follows:

“Canadian
sentencing jurisprudence has traditionally focussed (sic) on

the
aims of denunciation, deterrence, separation, and rehabilitation,

with
rehabilitation a relative late-comer to the sentencing analysis:

see

Gladue
, at para. 42.  With the introduction of Bill C-41, however,

Parliament
has placed new emphasis upon the goals of restorative

justice.
Section 718 sets out the fundamental purpose of sentencing,

as
well as the various sentencing objectives that should be vindicated

when
sanctions are imposed.  In
Gladue
,
supra
, Cory and Iacobucci

J.J.
stated at (para. 43):

Clearly
s. 718 is, in part, a restatement of the basic sentencing aims,

which
are listed in paras. (a) through (d).  What are new, though, are

paras.
(e) and (f), which along with para. (d) focus on the restorative

goals
of repairing the harms suffered by individual victims and by the

community
as a whole, promoting a sense of responsibility and an

acknowledgment
of the harm caused on the part of the offender, and

attempting
to rehabilitate or heal the offender.  The concept of

restorative
justice which underpins paras. (d), (e), and (f) is briefly

discussed
below, but as a general matter restorative justice involves

some
form of restitution and reintegration into the community.  The

need
for offenders to take responsibility for their actions is central

to
the sentencing process...Restorative sentencing goals do not usually

correlate
with the use of prison as a sanction.  In our view, Parliament
’
s

choice
to include (e) and (f) alongside the traditional sentencing goals

must
be understood as evidencing an intention to expand the parameters

of
the sentencing analysis for all offenders [Emphasis added; citation

omitted.]

Parliament
has mandated that expanded use be made of restorative

principles
in sentencing as a result of the general failure of incarceration

to
rehabilitate offenders and reintegrate them into society.  By placing

a
new emphasis on restorative principles, Parliament expects both to

reduce
the rate of incarceration and improve the effectiveness of

sentencing...”

[
37
]   In R. v.
Proulx
,
supra
the Court held  there are four criteria a Court must consider before
deciding to impose a conditional sentence:  (1) the offence must be one that is
not punishable by a minimum term of imprisonment; (2) the court must impose a
term of imprisonment of less than two years; (3) the safety of the community
would not be endangered by the offender serving the sentence in the community;
and (4) a conditional sentence would be consistent with the fundamental purpose
and principles

of sentencing set out in ss. 718  to 718.2.

[
38
]   Dealing with the
first condition, the offenses before the Court do not call for minimum terms of
imprisonment.  Dealing with the third condition, namely the safety of the
community, I am satisfied this accused does not pose a serious risk to the
community.  The
Proulx, supra
decision instructed the courts to consider
two factors in assessing the safety of the community, firstly, the risk of the
offender reoffending and secondly, the gravity of the damage that could ensue
in the event of reoffense.  In the case before me I believe the accused has
learned from his poor judgment and that the time spent in pretrial custody has
had a considerable effect in terms of deterring him from reoffending.  However,
I recognize that his family instability in the past will present some
challenges for him in future, but in the event this instability results in
reoffending these will not be the type of offenses which create safety concerns
to the community, even in terms of economic harm.  I do not expect the accused
to re-offend in future, but if I am wrong his transgressions will likely be
minor in nature.  From the evidence before me the accused is not prone to
violence or sophisticated schemes of dishonesty.  Even in his robbery attempt
his efforts to frighten were decidedly unsuccessful and so unsophisticated as
to be absurd.  He ended up having three people chasing him and discarding the
money in the parking lot.

[
39
]   In considering the
risk to the community, I also note the accused’s motives were to save his father’s
failing business and the offenses took place at a time when the accused had
been told to leave home having nowhere else to go than to a family who the
accused allowed to influence him toward criminal behavior.

[
40
]   Dealing with the
second condition, namely that the Court must determine the sentence ought not
to be a penitentiary term or a probationary one, it is clear to me, given the
nature of the offense, that a probationary term would be too lenient.  As to a
penitentiary term, I have considered a number of factors.  I have considered
the fact  the accused was 18 years old at the time of the robbery with only a
relatively minor youth court record and the complete absence of an adult
record.  I have also considered the unsophisticated nature of the offense which
was destined to failure from the outset.  While the note contained a threat of
violence, the teller herself at the time of the robbery thought the accused
very young and that he was ruining his life.  The accused was chased by three
people from the bank, threw the money into the parking lot and has received no
personal gain from the robbery itself.  I have also taken into account that the
accused has spent four months in pretrial custody, when he has never been in
gaol before at any time in his life.  I have considered his guilty pleas and
the fact the motive for the robbery was the accused’s desire to rescue his father’s business as opposed to the motive of greed which
is often seen in cases of this kind.  I have also taken into account the
personal circumstances of the accused at the time of the offenses before the
Court, namely that he had been required to leave his home with nowhere to go
except to a family who influenced him toward criminal activity.  I have also
considered that the accused is genuinely remorseful for his actions and accepts
full responsibility.  Taking all of this into account I have determined that a
proper sentence in this case would be a term of incarceration of two years less
a day globally.  Therefore all three of the statutory prerequisites for a
conditional sentence are met in this case. The question then becomes whether a
conditional sentence would be appropriate.

[
41
]   In making my
decision  this Court has been told by the Supreme Court  in the
Proulx,
supra
decision to ensure  a conditional sentence would be consistent with
the fundamental purpose and principles of sentencing set out in ss. 718 to
718.2 of the Code.  The Court held a conditional sentence is available in
principle for all offenses in which the statutory prerequisites are satisfied
and each case must be considered individually.  The Court also went further and
held  there is no presumption for or against the use of a conditional sentence
for particular offenses.  Indeed, the Court said it would be reversible error
not to consider the appropriateness of a conditional sentence where the
statutory prerequisites have been met.

[
42
]   Because the offense
before the Court  involves a robbery of a financial institution I have carefully
considered whether a conditional sentence would be appropriate.  The need to
denounce such activity and to protect financial institutions is of grave
concern to this court.  It would be unusual for this Court to consider a
conditional sentence appropriate for this type of offense.  However, this is
not a case where greed was the primary motive, nor was this a sophisticated
effort, or even one which had a serious chance of succeeding.  The
investigating officer describes the offense as more or less destined to fail
from the outset.  In the circumstances of this case, I believe it important to
consider whether a conditional sentence is appropriate to this case.

[
43
]   The Court  in
R.
v. Proulx
, supra
also held that to the extent  both punitive and
restorative objectives can be achieved in a given case, a conditional sentence
is likely a better sanction than incarceration.  Furthermore, the Court  held
that  although incarceration will usually provide more denunciation, a
conditional sentence can still provide a significant amount, particularly when
onerous conditions are imposed and the duration of the conditional sentence is
extended beyond the duration of the gaol  sentence that would ordinarily have
been imposed.  Since the sentence I have considered appropriate is two years
less a day, this Court cannot extend the conditional sentence beyond the
duration of a gaol sentence that would ordinarily have been imposed.  This is
because the conditional sentence order permitted by the legislation can only
extend for a period of two years less a day.  It may be, however, that through
the combination of a conditional sentence order and a probation order taking
effect upon the expiry of a conditional sentence order, a similar result can be
achieved.  It is open to this Court to impose conditions upon the accused
restricting his liberty throughout the two year time frame of the conditional
sentence order and continuing to restrict his liberty throughout a probation
order for an additional year.  In the result restrictions upon the accused’s liberty can be extended beyond the duration of the
original gaol sentence.

[
44
]  Finally, on the
subject of deterrence and denunciation and the comparison of the effectiveness
of incarceration versus conditional sentence in achieving these objectives, the
Supreme Court held in
Proulx, supra
that although incarceration
generally provides more deterrence than a conditional sentence, judges should
be wary of placing too much weight on deterrence given  the uncertain deterrent
effect of incarceration.  This last guidance from the Court has great
application to this Court with respect to specific deterrence in this case.
This youthful offender may well be harmed by post trial incarceration where he
experiences and possibly will learn from the general prison population.  So far
he has been held in the remand centre where he is not among the general prison
population and has not had the opportunity to be influenced to any significant
degree by his fellow prisoners.  His physical appearance  will also work
against him in a prison setting, where the possibility of bullying and worse
exists.  Indeed, this young man may well come out of prison much worse than
when he went in, thereby becoming a greater risk to society as a result of his
having been incarcerated.

[
45
]   In assessing the
appropriateness of a conditional sentence order, the Supreme Court indicated a
need to consider whether conditions can be crafted which would be sufficiently
onerous as to provide deterrence as required by the sentencing principles in
the Code.  The need to consider what conditions would accomplish this objective
was also called for by the Court of Appeal of Alberta in the decision of
R.
v.

Millward
(an oral judgment of the Court rendered October 23, 2000
and filed in written form November 23, 2000).  There the Court held the trial
judge had erred in concluding a conditional sentence was appropriate before
even considering the terms of  the conditional sentence.  In the
Millward

decision the Court of Appeal was dealing with a $350,000.00 breach of trust
case in which the accused was motivated by greed.  The Court held a conditional
sentence order inappropriate in those circumstances.

[
46
]    I have also considered the
R. v.
Watkinson
decision rendered by the Court of

Appeal on March 30
th
,
2001.  In that case the Court dealt with a breach of trust theft from an
employer in the amount of approximately $118,000.00 along with a charge under
Section 426(1) of the Code involving the acceptance of secret commissions
totaling some $16,000.00.  In the
Watkinson
decision the Court of Appeal
considered that a conditional sentence order was appropriate in the
circumstances of that case, relying upon a number of cases including the
decision of
R. v. Proulx
, supra
.  The Court also held the denunciatory
effect of forcing the appellant to live in the community under strict control
should not be underestimated in terms of assessing the denunciatory and
deterrent value of a conditional sentence order.  The Court stated that serving
the sentence in the community involves an accused “bearing the stigma of her crime on a daily basis in
plain view of her peers.”

[
47
]   In the case before me I am of the view there
would be some denunciatory and

deterrent effect upon this
accused by requiring him to serve his gaol sentence in the community in the
plain view of those with whom he is in contact.  He is concerned about the
shame his actions have brought upon his family.    My limited assessment of
this accused is that the stigma created by such a sentence would indeed deter
him from further reoffending, although I also believe there has also been
significant deterrent value to date as a result of his involvement with the
criminal justice system, and in particular the four months he has spent in
pretrial custody.

[
48
]   In the case before me, I am of the view that
further denunciatory and deterrent value

would occur through the
curtailment of the accused’s freedom
not only for the two years of the conditional sentence, but also for an
additional year of probation to follow the conditional sentence order.  The
orders might restrict the accused’s
liberty  by requiring him to remain in his residence at all times unless he is
at work or permitted to leave his home for other necessary reasons approved in
writing by his probation officer.  This curtailment of his liberty would
include both day and night, seven days a week.  His residence would also have
to be approved in writing by his supervisor, and preferably the accused ought
to be required to reside with his parents at least for time being.

[
49
]   The importance of the probation order to
follow  the conditional sentence order is

that the same restrictions
on the accused’s freedom could be
placed into the probation order, thus ensuring that effectively the accused’s freedoms are severely restricted for a full three
years.  Thus, the objectives of denunciation and deterrence in sentencing for
the serious nature of the offense before the Court can also be addressed in
this way.  While the consequences of breaching the probation order are not as
direct as the breach of a conditional sentence order, options available to a
sentencing judge on  a breach of probation would include a custodial term as
well as a further and extended conditional sentence order.  Either of these
options would be reasonable when the background for the existence of the
probation order is understood to be that the Court wishes to curtail the
accused’s liberty for longer than the
two years less a day sentence considered appropriate in this case.  Not only
would this Court wish to impose onerous conditions on the accused (as referred
to in the

Proulx, supra

decision), but also the Court would seek to have
them continue for a longer time frame than the  two years less a day length of
sentence the Court considers appropriate in this case.  I recognize that the

Proulx, supra
decision held the extension of a conditional sentence order
for a longer time frame than the offence would normally attract was one way to
address the objectives of denunciation and deterrence set forth in the
sentencing principles contained in the Code.  I also recognize that my proposal
to add a probationary order after the conditional sentence order is not the
same thing and I have already mentioned my recognition of the different
consequences which flow from a conditional sentence order and a probation
order.  However, in the case before me, since the offenses themselves would
attract just under two years incarceration, it is not open to this Court to add
to the appropriate length of sentence by means of a conditional sentence order,
but similar objectives can be secured through the use of a probationary order
to take effect upon the expiration of the two year conditional sentence order
itself.

[
50
]   It is also open to this Court to direct that
any breach of the probation order come

back before this Court
(meaning this Judge) in the event of a guilty plea to that offense, a practice
which is not unusual in cases where the background of a particular order may be
best  understood by the original sentencing Judge.

[
51
]   Since restorative justice involves some form
of restitution and reintegration into

the community, any
conditional sentence order considered appropriate in this case would also
require the accused to make restitution in the amount of $1,547.00,
representing the shortfall of the stolen money thrown in the parking lot.  The
accused would also be required to obtain and maintain employment or attend an
educational institution on a full-time basis.  He would also be required to
attend for assessment and complete such counseling or treatment for anger
management and other psychological matters which may be present as a result of
his chaotic family background, it being my belief that the poor judgment
exercised by him and the willingness to please those who had taken him in
through criminal conduct are matters which are the result of his own emotional
insecurities.  To overcome these less than obvious motivators of his behavior,
he may well need professional help.  Finally some 240 hours of community
service work ought to be required of the accused in order to also address the
need for deterrence with respect to the robbery of a financial institution.

SUMMARY AND
CONCLUSIONS

[
52
]   The issue before the Court is whether a
conditional sentence order is appropriate

given the serious nature of
the offenses before the Court, in particular the robbery of a financial
institution.   On the basis of the decision of
R. v. Proulx
, supra
there
are four criteria a Court must consider before deciding to impose a conditional
sentence.  The first three are statutory prerequisites and they are as
follows:  Firstly, the offence must be one that is not punishable by a minimum
term of imprisonment.  In the case before the Court none of the offenses are
punishable by minimum terms of imprisonment, thus satisfying the first  of the
four criterion referred to in
R. v. Proulx
, supra
.

[
53
]   Secondly, the Court must impose a term of
imprisonment of less than two years.

While normally the robbery
of a financial institution would not meet this criterion, the specific
circumstances of this case are such that I have determined this second
criterion is met as well.  In making this determination I have considered the
aggravating  and mitigating factors earlier referred to in this decision and in
particular I note the accused was 18 years old at the time of offence with a
relatively minor youth court  record.  The circumstances of the offenses
themselves were extremely unsophisticated and, in the words of the
investigating officer, more or less destined to fail from the outset.  In
addition, the accused was not motivated by greed, but rather by his misguided
attempt to rescue his father’s failing
hair salon business.  The offenses before the Court all took place over a time
period during which the accused had been forced to leave his parents’ home and had nowhere to go.  He was taken in by a
family whose negative influence upon him throughout this time frame resulted in
criminal activity.  I have also considered the fact the accused has spent some
four months  in pretrial custody,  and he has never been in custody before.
The youth court record indicates the accused has had two probationary sentences
in the past.  I have considered the fact  the accused is genuinely remorseful
and prepared to accept the consequences of his actions, even if it means a
penitentiary term.  He takes sole responsibility for his actions.

[
54
]      In my deliberations concerning this second
criterion, I have also taken into

account that in my view a
penitentiary term for this particular accused could well produce more harm than
good to society in the sense that he may well come out of a penitentiary much
more dangerous to society than when he went in.  This is because of his age and
his slight physical characteristics, which may continue to make him to make him
a target of bullying, as has occurred in his past.  The accused now appears to
be a candidate for rehabilitation.  I am concerned this may not be the case if
he is exposed to the peer pressure of the inmates in a penitentiary.  The
Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Proulx
, supra
indicated that trial
judges ought to be wary of placing too much weight on deterrence given the
uncertain effects of incarceration.

[
55
]      With respect to the third criterion,
namely being satisfied  allowing the accused

to serve a sentence in the
community would not endanger the community either in the physical or economic
sense, I have determined this criterion has been met in the circumstances of
this case.  I am satisfied this accused does not pose a serious risk to the
community.  I do not expect him to reoffend, but if I am wrong it is my
assessment his transgressions will likely be minor in nature.  I have expressed
the view the instability of his family background will present some challenges
for him to overcome in the future and it is only for this reason that I mention
any possibility of reoffending.

[
56
]      Having determined  the three statutory
prerequisites have been met, it is my

duty to consider whether
the granting of a conditional sentence order would be appropriate in this case,
and in particular whether the objectives of denunciation and deterrence
required by the seriousness of the offence can be adequately met by the imposition
of a conditional sentence order.  In my judgment the objectives of denunciation
and deterrence required in this sentencing can be combined with a restorative
sentence effectively.  The decision of
R. v. Proulx
, supra
held that
where both punitive and restorative objectives can be achieved in a given case,
a conditional sentence is likely a better sanction than incarceration.  In my
view that is so in the circumstances of this case.  Significant denunciation
and deterrence can be provided in a conditional sentence order which entirely
restricts the accused’s liberty day and
night, seven days a week not only for the term of the conditional sentence
order, but also for an additional year thereafter in accordance with a
probation order to take effect upon the expiration of the conditional sentence
order itself.  The curtailment of the accused’s liberty in both a conditional sentence order and the probation order
would be such that the accused would be required to remain in his residence (a
residence which would have to be approved in writing by his supervisor) with
the exception of being permitted to leave his residence for purposes of work,
education or other necessities approved in writing by his supervisor.  The
curtailment of liberty would apply at all times during the existence of both
orders.

[
57
]      In addition, the objectives of deterrence
and denunciation (along with restitution

and restoration) could be
addressed by requiring the accused to pay restitution in the sum of $1,547.00
and to attend for assessment  and complete such counseling or treatment for
anger management or other psychological matters as directed.  In addition the
accused could be required to perform some 240 hours of community service work
prior to the expiration of the conditional sentence order.  As suggested in
Watkinson,
supra
, the stigma created by this accused having to serve such an onerous
conditional sentence order in the community is significant, since he will daily
be observed by his peers to be serving a gaol sentence in the community.

[
58
]      Such a sentence would permit this accused
to work or educate himself by

remaining in the
community.  It would have the decided advantage of not exposing this young man
to the negative influence of prison.  The accused has significant family
support and I do not categorize him as an individual who must be separated from
society in order to ensure its protection.  On the contrary my assessment of
this accused is that he can become a productive member of society and it is
preferable to restore this individual by permitting him to serve his sentence
in the community rather than an institution.

[
59
]      I invite both counsel to address the Court
with respect to any terms of either the

conditional sentence order
or probation order I have mentioned in the event there are other matters either
counsel believe ought to be addressed in addition to those terms which I have
already indicated are necessary in order to address the objectives of
deterrence and denunciation required because of the nature of the offenses
before the Court.  I anticipate the final sentence in this case will be a
conditional sentence for a period of two years less a day followed by a term of
probation for a period of one year.  I have already discussed the necessary
terms of both orders, and I will finalize both orders after hearing from
counsel.

[
60
]      I wish to thank both counsel for their
submissions with respect to this case.

[
61
]      DATED in the City of Calgary, Province of
Alberta, this 19
th
day of April,
